payload.claim_text: Types of bus lanes include: curbside bus lanes (travel lanes for buses at the curb, no parking/standing during hours in effect), offset bus lanes (one lane away from curb, parking still possible), center-running or median bus lanes (middle of roadway, e.g. Woodhaven Boulevard, Kings Highway, 161st Street; vehicles cannot enter for any reason while in effect), and busways (whole roadway allocated to buses and local access).
payload.description: Four types of bus lanes described in the brochure

raw_text: Curbside bus lanes: are travel lanes for buses at the curb. Parking and standing at the curb are not allowed during the hours the bus lane is in effect. Offset bus lanes: are travel lanes for buses one lane away from the curb. This makes parking or standing at the curb still possible. Center-running or median bus lanes: are in the middle of the roadway, such as Woodhaven Boulevard, Kings Highway, and 161st Street. Vehicles are not permitted to enter the bus lanes for any reason while the bus lane is in effect. Busways: allocate the whole roadway to buses and local access.

payload.claim_text: Generally, the calendarization of monthly debt service deposits is calculated by dividing projected annual debt service by 12. Month to month variations ('timing differences') on the existing debt portfolio can occur based upon, among other things, (a) for all bonds, the date when income from the securities in which the debt service accounts are invested becomes available varies, (b) for variable rate financings, differences between (i) the budgeted interest rate and the actual interest rate, (ii) projected interest payment dates to bondholders and actual interest payment dates to bondholders, and (iii) projected monthly funding dates for accrued debt service and actual funding dates, (c) for transactions with swaps, the difference between when MTA/TBTA funds debt service and the receipt of the corresponding swap payment by the counterparty, and difference between rates received and rates paid and (d) for commercial paper, the interest payment date is the date of the maturity of the commercial paper and the dealers set the term of the commercial paper from 1 to 270 days, which is not foreseeable at the time the annual debt service budgets are prepared.
payload.subject: Calendarization of monthly debt service deposits

Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies.
payload.description: Definition of the farebox recovery ratio metric as used by MTA.

raw_text: Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year, except in an accounting-ledger sense, but are, in effect, passed on to future years. Those costs include depreciation and interest on long-term debt. Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies. That is why MTA operating statements generally show deficits. In addition, the recovery ratio allocates centralized MTA services to the Agencies, such as Security, the costs of the Inspector General, Civil Rights, Audit, Risk Management, Legal and Shared Services.

display_name: MTA Equity Framework and Title VI

payload.claim_text: Recognizing the presence of historically disadvantaged populations helps ensure that resources are invested, either through allocation or reallocation, and protected within these communities to reduce obstacles to transit access.
payload.statement: MTA's equity framework uses Title VI status and broader socioeconomic factors: transit dependency, minority representation, income, access to opportunity, and mobility needs.

payload.claim_text: A detailed Equity Score Index was developed using the MTA equity framework indicators. This index assigned Equity Scores to geographies, facilitating an evaluation of differences between the existing and proposed Queens bus network. Equity Scores were then categorized into three distinct tiers.

Tier 1: Significant Equity Consideration represents areas where transit-dependent populations, historically underserved communities, and/or those facing systemic inequities are most concentrated. Tier 2: Moderate Equity Consideration includes areas with notable, though less severe, equity challenges. Tier 3: Low Equity Consideration encompasses areas with comparatively lower equity-related concerns.

payload.claim_text: Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year, except in an accounting-ledger sense, but are, in effect, passed on to future years. Those costs include depreciation and interest on long-term debt. Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies. That is why MTA operating statements generally show deficits. In addition, the recovery ratio allocates centralized MTA services to the Agencies, such as Security, the costs of the Inspector General, Civil Rights, Audit, Risk Management, Legal and Shared Services.

Monthly hedges are equal to approximately 4% of the projected fuel purchases expected to occur 13-24 months from each hedge execution date. The actual percentage hedged could be higher or lower than the 50% target depending on the actual levels of fuel consumption. While the fuel hedging program includes compressed natural gas, there are currently no active hedges.

To fulfill its purpose, the Committee shall: 1. monitor and update the Board Chair and the Board on the operating performance of the LIRR/LIB, including information on railroad, bus and paratransit service; 2. monitor and update the Board Chair and the Board on the safety record of LIRR/LIB; such monitoring shall include reviewing and monitoring customer and employee safety; 3. monitor and update the Board Chair and the Board on the implementation of security programs pertaining to LIRR/LIB operations and facilities; 4. monitor and update the Board Chair and the Board on the finances of the LIRR/LIB, including financial reports, ridership reports, and the use of LIRR/LIB funds; 5. review and make recommendations to the Board Chair and the Board regarding proposed procurement contracts of the LIRR/LIB that require Board approval; 6. review and make recommendations to the Board Chair and the Board on proposed capital projects of the LIRR/LIB and monitor the status of such projects

The Committee shall: 7. review and make recommendations to the Board Chair and the Board regarding service and policy changes that require Board approval; 8. facilitate the identification of approaches and solutions that address LIRR/LIB security issues, including best practices in national and international security respecting transportation operations and facilities and review and make recommendations to the Board Chair and the Board regarding LIRR/LIB security issues; and 9. review periodically with the Counsel of the MTA, the Chief Compliance Officer, and the Counsel of the LIRR/LIB: (i) legal and regulatory matters that may have a material impact on the LIRR/LIB; and (ii) the scope and effectiveness of compliance policies and programs.

Materials and Supplies were $5.9 million unfavorable primarily due to pooled materials charge out, miscellaneous inventory adjustment and right of way materials. display_name: Central Business District Tolling Program update

payload.claim_text: The Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP) was authorized by the MTA Reform and Traffic Mobility Act and enacted in April 2019. On June 27, 2023, the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) issued a Finding of No Significant Impact. The Traffic Mobility Review Board (TMRB) held its first meeting on July 19, 2023. Contractors have up to 310 days from the federal approval to complete the design, development, testing, and installation of the tolling system and equipment.

On August 20, 2023, fare increases went into effect across MTA subways, buses, and commuter railroads. With additional funding from New York State, the MTA was able to keep the fare increase to 4%. This was the first fare increase since 2019 and the first increase in the base subway and bus fare since 2015.

In January of 2023, the Grand Central Madison terminal was opened for LIRR service. Service was initially run as a shuttle between Jamaica and Grand Central Madison terminals. Full LIRR service to Grand Central Madison began in February, resulting in a 41% increase in overall LIRR service.

As of June 30, 2022, MTA Bus Company has 3,782 employees, approximately 3,665 of whom are represented by three different unions (now including the United Transit Leadership Organization) and five bargaining units.

Farebox operating ratio focuses on Agency operating financial performance. It reflects the way MTA meets its statutory and bond-covenant budget-balancing requirements, and it excludes certain costs that are not subject to Agency control, but are provided centrally by the MTA.

Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year, except in an accounting-ledger sense, but are, in effect, passed on to future years. Those costs include depreciation and interest on long-term debt. Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies. That is why MTA operating statements generally show deficits. In addition, the recovery ratio allocates centralized MTA services to the Agencies, such as Security, the costs of the Inspector General, Civil Rights, Audit, Risk Management, Legal and Shared Services.

payload.claim_text: Generally, the calendarization of monthly debt service deposits is calculated by dividing projected annual debt service by 12. Month to month variations ('timing differences') on the existing debt portfolio can occur based upon, among other things, (a) for all bonds, the date when income from the securities in which the debt service accounts are invested becomes available varies, (b) for variable rate financings, differences between the budgeted interest rate and the actual interest rate, projected interest payment dates to bondholders and actual interest payment dates, and projected monthly funding dates for accrued debt service and actual funding dates, (c) for transactions with swaps, the difference between when MTA/TBTA funds debt service and the receipt of the corresponding swap payment by the counterparty, and difference between rates received and rates paid and (d) for commercial paper, the interest payment date is the date of the maturity of the commercial paper and the dealers set the term of the commercial paper from 1 to 270 days.

payload.claim_text: Farebox operating ratio focuses on Agency operating financial performance. It reflects the way MTA meets its statutory and bond-covenant budget-balancing requirements, and it excludes certain costs that are not subject to Agency control, but are provided centrally by the MTA.
payload.description: Definition of the farebox operating ratio focusing on Agency operating financial performance
payload.subject: Farebox operating ratio

payload.claim_text: Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year, except in an accounting-ledger sense, but are, in effect, passed on to future years. Those costs include depreciation and interest on long-term debt. Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies. That is why MTA operating statements generally show deficits. In addition, the recovery ratio allocates centralized MTA services to the Agencies, such as Security, the costs of the Inspector General, Civil Rights, Audit, Risk Management, Legal and Shared Services.
payload.description: Definition of the farebox recovery ratio and its long-term focus

payload.claim_text: Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year, except in an accounting-ledger sense, but are, in effect, passed on to future years. Those costs include depreciation and interest on long-term debt. Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies. That is why MTA operating statements generally show deficits. In addition, the recovery ratio allocates centralized MTA services to the Agencies, such as Security, the costs of the Inspector General, Civil Rights, Audit, Risk Management, Legal and Shared Services.

payload.claim_text: Alcohol advertising remains prohibited category but is now allowed in limited settings: digital displays outside student commutation hours; static displays in major commuter rail hubs and stations near large venues; train wrap on S shuttle only; and billboards with 500-foot certification.
payload.subject: alcohol advertising

raw_text: Third, the updated policy maintains alcohol advertising in the policy's "Prohibited" category, while also now allowing for alcohol advertising in the following limited settings: - On digital displays within stations or attached to station exteriors, and on the interior of railcars and buses, but only outside of typical student commutation hours (6-8 a.m. and 2-5 p.m. on weekdays when school is in session); - On static displays inside (1) major commuter rail hubs and (2) stations adjacent to large venues where alcohol is lawfully sold; - In "train wrap" format on the S shuttle train between Times Square and Grand Central – but not on the exterior of any other MTA railcars or buses; and - On billboards, but only where the advertiser certifies that such billboards are not readable within 500 feet of a school, playground, or place of worship.

display_name: Final Determination Reassignment to Chief Administrative Officer

payload.claim_text: Final determinations regarding Advertising Committee decisions will now be made by the MTA's Chief Administrative Officer or their designee, reassigned from previous authority.
payload.subject: final determination authority

raw_text: Fourth, the updated advertising policy reassigns within the MTA the responsibility to issue final determinations regarding decisions by the MTA's Advertising Committee. Advertisers can request a final determination after the committee rejects an ad pursuant to the Advertising Policy. Such final determinations will now be made by the MTA's Chief Administrative Officer or their designee.

payload.claim_text: Large Format Advertising includes (i) advertising that physically wraps exterior surfaces of subway cars, train cars, or buses and (ii) any other equivalent or greater sized advertisement. Advertisements prominently displaying the unclothed human body will not be accepted in such formats.
payload.subject: Large Format Advertising

raw_text: Second, the updated policy clarifies the requirements for proposed "Large Format Advertising." This format includes (i) advertising that physically "wraps" and so covers all or nearly all of the exterior surfaces of subway cars, train cars, or buses and (ii) any other advertisement in any medium that appears on MTA Property that is an equivalent or greater size. Any advertising which prominently displays the unclothed human body, regardless of the nature of any clothing items depicted, will not be accepted in such formats.

payload.claim_text: In 2025 year to date, approximately 89% of the fare evasion offenses resulted in warnings.

On January 1, 2025, the fine structure for fare evasion violations changed. Fines for fare evasion are now based on the number of violations committed during a four-year period: Warning (first offense) - no fine; Tier 2 (second offense) - $100 fine ($50 for Fair Fare NYC participants); Tier 3 (third offense) - $150 fine ($75 for Fair Fare NYC participants). Those who pay on time in full receive a $50 credit on an OMNY card for full-fare customers or a $25 credit on an OMNY card for Fair Fare NYC participants.
A case is adjudicated when a respondent requests a hearing, and a determination is made by a hearing officer.

Monthly hedges are equal to approximately 4% of the projected fuel purchases expected to occur 13-24 months from each hedge execution date. display_name: Leaf season slip/slide events impact on rail operations

payload.claim_text: Following each leaf season, typically from early October to late November, the Railroads have historically experienced slip/slide events due to contamination of the rail by leaf debris. This reduces the level of adhesion between the rail and train wheel, and adversely affects a train's ability to stop, resulting in damage to wheels in the form of flat spots. The resulting wheel damage requires removing passenger cars and locomotives from service for repair, thereby causing delays, and shorter or canceled trains.

LIRR continued to protect its infrastructure with numerous state-of-good-repair projects this year, while also making significant progress in moving to 100% accessibility. St. Albans Station debuted its elevator in November, while Laurelton and Locust Manor stations will have new elevators this month, making LIRR stations 93% accessible by the end of the year.

raw_text: The federal funding, however, masks the structural imbalance in MTA's finances. And with federal funding exhausted in 2025 and only $1.5 billion remaining in deficit borrowing proceeds, 2026 will likely be significantly out of balance without actions to address the structural imbalance.

payload.claim_text: Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year, except in an accounting-ledger sense, but are, in effect, passed on to future years. Those costs include depreciation and interest on long-term debt. Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies. That is why MTA operating statements generally show deficits. In addition, the recovery ratio allocates centralized MTA services to the Agencies, such as Security, the costs of the Inspector General, Civil Rights, Audit, Risk Management, Legal and Shared Services.

payload.claim_text: Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year, except in an accounting-ledger sense, but are, in effect, passed on to future years; those costs include depreciation and interest on long-term debt. In addition, the recovery ratio allocates centralized MTA services to the Agencies, such as Security, the costs of the Inspector General, Civil Rights, Audit, Risk Management, Legal and Shared Services.

Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year, except in an accounting-ledger sense, but are, in effect, passed on to future years. Those costs include depreciation and interest on long-term debt. Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies. That is why MTA operating statements generally show deficits. In addition, the recovery ratio allocates centralized MTA services to the Agencies, such as Security, the costs of the Inspector General, Civil Rights, Audit, Risk Management, Legal and Shared Services.

Farebox recovery ratio has a long-term focus. It includes costs that are not funded in the current year...including depreciation and interest on long-term debt. Approximately 20% (and sometimes more) of MTA costs are not recovered in the current year from farebox revenues, other operating revenues or subsidies.

payload.claim_text: Select Bus Service (SBS) is a joint program between MTA New York City Transit (NYCT) and the New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT), which aims to improve transit service through the application of Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) principles to New York City's busiest bus routes.
payload.statement: SBS Program Definition

payload.claim_text: Six new SBS services were implemented since 2008 (along with M60 SBS coming in Spring 2014). The chief goal of the SBS program is to make buses faster, more reliable and easily identified as a premium service. SBS serves all five boroughs, focusing on high-ridership bus routes. SBS routes are complementary to the city's subway system. Each SBS project has included extensive public engagement involving community boards, business improvement districts, merchant associations, civic groups and officials. Dedicated bus lanes, off-board fare payment, transit signal priority and branding are the key elements. NYCDOT and NYCT focused on fast implementation within constrained rights-of-way. These projects have led to up to 20% faster bus service and 10-20% increases in corridor ridership in the first year.
